notes.title: Matter — P. Sharma, extension
notes.content:
Employment-based extension. Filed 2 February, receipt notice 11 February. Current processing at this service centre is running 4 to 7 months.

Statutory deadline for the current authorisation is 30 September. Premium processing is available and the client has not asked for it.

The employer is the payer. The client is the individual. Those are different people and the file goes to one of them.

notes.title: Who the client is when a company pays
notes.content:
The most common misunderstanding in this practice.

The company pays and receives an invoice. The individual is the client and receives everything else. HR is entitled to know that a filing was made because they signed the petition. They are not entitled to status, stage, correspondence, or history.

I have had this conversation with every employer I have worked with, without exception.

notes.title: Employer request log
notes.content:
TechFlow HR has asked twice for a status update on an individual matter. Both times I have given the same answer: I will confirm that a filing exists because they signed it, and nothing further.

The second request came framed as needing it for headcount planning. The framing does not change the answer.

notes.title: Processing times — current
notes.content:
Shareable. Service centre is at 4 to 7 months for this category, up from 3 to 5 last year. Premium processing brings it to 15 business days at additional cost.

Anyone can look this up; I say it plainly so nobody thinks I am being difficult when I decline the individual question.

notes.title: Deadline calendar — Q2 and Q3
notes.content:
Four matters with statutory deadlines before October. One of them is tight enough that premium processing stops being optional in June.

The individual needs to decide that, not the employer, and not me.

notes.title: Caseload — current
notes.content:
Twenty-three active matters across eleven employers. Mostly extensions and transfers, three permanent residence, one appeal.

Sole practice means the caseload is the constraint and I turn work away roughly monthly.

notes.title: Processing times — tracking
notes.content:
I track published times by service centre and category because clients ask and because the published number and the observed number diverge by weeks.

Current divergence is about three weeks longer than published, consistently.

notes.title: Premium processing — when it is worth it
notes.content:
When a deadline is inside the standard window, when a start date depends on it, or when the anxiety is costing the client more than the fee.

The third reason is real and rarely stated out loud.

notes.title: Requests for evidence — patterns
notes.content:
About one in five filings draws one. The pattern this year is specialty occupation challenges on roles with generic titles.

The fix is at the petition-drafting stage: a title that describes the work rather than a job ladder rung.

notes.title: Employer education
notes.content:
Every new employer relationship starts with the same conversation about who the client is.

HR teams are not being difficult. They genuinely believe that paying means receiving, and in every other professional service they buy, it does.

notes.title: Appeal — one active
notes.content:
One matter on appeal. Slow, expensive, and the client is carrying it well.

Outcome distribution on this category is not encouraging and the client knows the numbers because I gave them.

notes.title: Fee structure
notes.content:
Flat fee by matter type plus government fees. Predictable for the employer, which is why they use me.

Complex matters lose money and I do them anyway when the client is decent.

notes.title: Regulatory change monitoring
notes.content:
Policy shifts faster than statute. A memorandum can change adjudication practice overnight without any change in law.

Sole practice means no research department, so this is me reading before the working day starts.

notes.title: Client communication — the anxiety problem
notes.content:
Immigration matters run for months with nothing to report. Silence reads as bad news.

Monthly status even when the status is 'no change' — the single highest-value thing I do that has nothing to do with law.

notes.title: File retention
notes.content: Seven years after matter close. Files contain identity documents, which makes retention a security question as much as a records one.

notes.title: Referral network
notes.content: Family immigration goes to a colleague, asylum goes elsewhere. Knowing what I do not do is most of a sole practice.

notes.title: Caseload
notes.content: Thirty-one active matters across eleven employers. Employment-based extensions are the bulk; four green card processes and two consular cases.

notes.title: Processing times — the running board
notes.content: Tracked by service centre and category, updated monthly from published data. Clients ask constantly and it is the one thing I can always answer.

notes.title: Requests for evidence — what triggers them
notes.content: Specialty occupation, wage level, and the employer-employee relationship, in that order. Most are answerable and add three months.

notes.title: Employer education — the recurring conversation
notes.content: Every new employer relationship starts with the same conversation about who the client is. Roughly a third do not fully accept it until the first time I decline a status request.

notes.title: Policy change tracking
notes.content: Two significant policy updates this year. Both changed evidentiary expectations without changing the regulation, which is the hardest kind to advise on.

notes.title: Consular processing — the unpredictable part
notes.content: Interview wait times at some posts run past a year. There is nothing to advise except plan around it, which is unsatisfying and true.

notes.title: Sole practitioner — capacity
notes.content: Thirty-one matters is near my ceiling. Taking a thirty-fifth means one of the existing ones gets less attention, which is the calculation nobody sees.

notes.title: Deadline discipline
notes.content: Statutory deadlines do not move. Everything in this practice is organised around a calendar that cannot be renegotiated, which makes it simpler than most law and less forgiving.

notes.title: Why I write to the client, not the employer
notes.content: Receipt notices, requests for evidence, approvals — all go to the individual. The employer gets an invoice and confirmation that a filing exists. Every time this has been blurred it has ended badly.

todos.title: Advise the client on premium processing before June
todos.content: Their decision. Give them the timeline and the cost and let them make it.

todos.title: Decline the HR status request again, in writing
todos.content: Second time. Put the payer-versus-client distinction on paper.

Invoice TechFlow for the quarter
todos.content: Amount only. No matter detail on the invoice.

todos.content: Even when the status is 'no change'. Silence reads as bad news.

todos.content: Specialty occupation challenges on generic titles.

todos.content: Three weeks longer than published, consistently.
